method: COMPILED FROM 2 SOURCES. S1: QUOTED from Norwegian Society of Rheumatology GCA working group (Haaversen et al.), Frontiers in Medicine 'Norwegian society of rheumatology recommendations on diagnosis and treatment of patients with giant cell arteritis' (published 6 January 2023 (volume 2022)), 16 claims; LICENCE: CC BY 4.0 (read at Europe PMC fullTextXML <license> element for PMC9853546). S2: PARAPHRASED AND HASH-ANCHORED from American College of Rheumatology and Vasculitis Foundation (Maz M, Chung SA, Abril A, et al.), Arthritis & Rheumatology 73(8):1349-1365 (doi 10.1002/art.41774), NIH author manuscript NIHMS2099608 '2021 American College of Rheumatology/Vasculitis Foundation Guideline for the Management of Giant Cell Arteritis and Takayasu Arteritis' (published online 8 July 2021), 11 claims; LICENCE: NIH author manuscript, not open access: 'This file is available for text mining. It may also be used consistent with the principles of fair use under the copyright law.' (read at NCBI efetch JATS XML <license> element for PMC12344528 (Europe PMC fullTextXML returned HTTP 500)). Verify each source separately: verify.py --source <file> --only-source S<n>. Edition 2.0 adds S2, the ACR/Vasculitis Foundation 2021 GCA guideline (NIH author manuscript, paraphrased and hash-anchored), because no readable Australian GCA guideline exists. Searches run 2026-09-24: PubMed for GCA with Australia/Australian/New Zealand or MJA/IMJ/Aust Prescr (2017-2026; only studies, a survey and a paywalled IMJ review); PMC for GCA/large-vessel vasculitis/PMR guidelines or recommendations (2020-2026). Only the GCA part of S2 is used; its Takayasu recommendations are not. S2's definitions table (glucocorticoid dose ranges) was not in the text. S1's claims are unchanged.

claims.claim: **GCA occurs almost only over age 50, peaking at 70 to 80 years, more often in women.** Subsets are cranial, large-vessel, or mixed.
claims.source_text: Giant cell arteritis occurs almost exclusively in people older than 50 years of age, with a peak in onset between 70 and 80 years of age and with a female predominance … The main subsets include isolated cranial arteritis (c-GCA), isolated large vessel vasculitis (LV-GCA), and coexisting cranial and large vessel vasculitis (mixed-GCA)
claims.locator: Norwegian Society of Rheumatology GCA working group (Haaversen et al.), Frontiers in Medicine, 'Norwegian society of rheumatology recommendations on diagnosis and treatment of patients with giant cell arteritis', published 6 January 2023 (volume 2022), https://europepmc.org/article/PMC/PMC9853546, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Ask about** polymyalgia symptoms, new headache, jaw or tongue claudication, visual disturbance, arm or leg claudication and constitutional symptoms. **Examine and test:** heart and lung auscultation, blood pressure in both arms, temperature, CRP, ESR and full blood count.
claims.source_text: In patients with suspected GCA, a thorough history should be obtained, including inquiry about polymyalgia symptoms, new-onset headache, tongue- or jaw-claudication, vision disturbances, arm or leg claudication, constitutional symptoms (fatigue, fever, and weight loss). Additionally, a thorough clinical examination and laboratory workup should be performed including heart and lung auscultation, blood pressure in both arms, temperature, C-reactive protein (CRP), erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR), and full blood count
claims.locator: Norwegian Society of Rheumatology GCA working group (Haaversen et al.), Frontiers in Medicine, 'Norwegian society of rheumatology recommendations on diagnosis and treatment of patients with giant cell arteritis', published 6 January 2023 (volume 2022), https://europepmc.org/article/PMC/PMC9853546, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Refer suspected GCA within 24 h** to a fast-track clinic or rheumatologist (or another relevant specialist if neither is available). Work-up must not delay treatment.
claims.source_text: Patients suspected of having GCA, should be directly referred to a Fast-Track Clinic (FTC) or a rheumatologist for further evaluation, treatment, and follow-up within 24 h. In cases where FTC- or rheumatology consult is unavailable within 24 h the patient may be referred to other relevant specialists (e.g., neurologist, ophthalmologist, and internist). … Diagnostic work-up should not delay the initiation of treatment.
claims.locator: Norwegian Society of Rheumatology GCA working group (Haaversen et al.), Frontiers in Medicine, 'Norwegian society of rheumatology recommendations on diagnosis and treatment of patients with giant cell arteritis', published 6 January 2023 (volume 2022), https://europepmc.org/article/PMC/PMC9853546, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Visual symptoms: refer to ophthalmology,** without delaying treatment.
claims.source_text: In patients with GCA and visual symptoms, referral to an ophthalmologist is highly recommended. Initiation of treatment should not be delayed while waiting for this evaluation
claims.locator: Norwegian Society of Rheumatology GCA working group (Haaversen et al.), Frontiers in Medicine, 'Norwegian society of rheumatology recommendations on diagnosis and treatment of patients with giant cell arteritis', published 6 January 2023 (volume 2022), https://europepmc.org/article/PMC/PMC9853546, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Ultrasound at least the temporal and axillary arteries** (experienced operator, high-end equipment); adding the facial artery raises sensitivity. If ultrasound is unavailable or inconclusive, consider temporal artery biopsy of >1 cm after fixation; giant cells are not obligatory.
claims.source_text: In patients with suspected GCA, ultrasound of at least temporal and axillary arteries () should be performed by an ultrasonographer experienced in vascular ultrasound using high-end ultrasound equipment () (Tables 2, 3). Ultrasound of the facial artery further increases the sensitivity to diagnose GCA (). If ultrasound is not available or inconclusive, a biopsy of the temporal artery should be considered. The length of the biopsy should be >1 cm after fixation. … Giant cells in the biopsy are not obligate for the diagnosis of GCA, but appropriate pathological findings should be present
claims.locator: Norwegian Society of Rheumatology GCA working group (Haaversen et al.), Frontiers in Medicine, 'Norwegian society of rheumatology recommendations on diagnosis and treatment of patients with giant cell arteritis', published 6 January 2023 (volume 2022), https://europepmc.org/article/PMC/PMC9853546, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Image the large vessels too** (ultrasound of carotid, vertebral and subclavian arteries, or CT, MRA or PET-CT): large-vessel involvement may mean difficult-to-treat disease, and temporal involvement carries more risk of visual loss.
claims.source_text: In addition, ultrasound of large vessels (carotid, vertebral, and subclavian) () or CT of large vessels or MRA or PET-CT depending on the availability is recommended. It is essential to recognize the disease extent as early as possible as large vessel involvement may indicate difficult-to-treat disease, while temporal artery involvement has been associated with a higher risk for visual loss
claims.locator: Norwegian Society of Rheumatology GCA working group (Haaversen et al.), Frontiers in Medicine, 'Norwegian society of rheumatology recommendations on diagnosis and treatment of patients with giant cell arteritis', published 6 January 2023 (volume 2022), https://europepmc.org/article/PMC/PMC9853546, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **High suspicion plus a positive test confirms GCA; low suspicion plus a negative test makes it unlikely.** Anything else needs individual assessment.
claims.source_text: In a patient with high clinical suspicion of GCA and a positive diagnostic test (biopsy or imaging modality), no further test is required to confirm the diagnosis. In patients with low clinical suspicion of GCA and a negative diagnostic test (biopsy or imaging modality), the probability for GCA is low. In other cases, an individual assessment will be necessary for further diagnostics.
claims.locator: Norwegian Society of Rheumatology GCA working group (Haaversen et al.), Frontiers in Medicine, 'Norwegian society of rheumatology recommendations on diagnosis and treatment of patients with giant cell arteritis', published 6 January 2023 (volume 2022), https://europepmc.org/article/PMC/PMC9853546, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **S2 (ACR, US) prefers temporal artery biopsy to ultrasound or cranial MRI for diagnosis,** because US ultrasound expertise is limited, results depend on the operator, and steroids quickly erase the signs; where the expertise exists, ultrasound is a useful complement.
claims.locator: American College of Rheumatology and Vasculitis Foundation (Maz M, Chung SA, Abril A, et al.), Arthritis & Rheumatology 73(8):1349-1365 (doi 10.1002/art.41774), NIH author manuscript NIHMS2099608, '2021 American College of Rheumatology/Vasculitis Foundation Guideline for the Management of Giant Cell Arteritis and Takayasu Arteritis', published online 8 July 2021, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12344528/, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: **Biopsy technique:** start with one side (take the other if symptoms are not one-sided, or the first is negative and doubt remains), take a long segment (>1 cm), and biopsy within two weeks of starting oral steroids; a later biopsy can still help.
claims.locator: American College of Rheumatology and Vasculitis Foundation (Maz M, Chung SA, Abril A, et al.), Arthritis & Rheumatology 73(8):1349-1365 (doi 10.1002/art.41774), NIH author manuscript NIHMS2099608, '2021 American College of Rheumatology/Vasculitis Foundation Guideline for the Management of Giant Cell Arteritis and Takayasu Arteritis', published online 8 July 2021, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12344528/, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: **Image the large vessels** after a negative biopsy, and at diagnosis in everyone (CT or MR angiography from neck to pelvis) as a baseline for aneurysm and stenosis follow-up.
claims.locator: American College of Rheumatology and Vasculitis Foundation (Maz M, Chung SA, Abril A, et al.), Arthritis & Rheumatology 73(8):1349-1365 (doi 10.1002/art.41774), NIH author manuscript NIHMS2099608, '2021 American College of Rheumatology/Vasculitis Foundation Guideline for the Management of Giant Cell Arteritis and Takayasu Arteritis', published online 8 July 2021, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12344528/, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Start glucocorticoids immediately on suspicion.** Prednisolone 40 mg/day without visual manifestations; 60 mg/day with visual involvement (visual loss, diplopia, amaurosis fugax, blurred vision). A single IV methylprednisolone 500 mg dose before 60 mg/day may be considered, though evidence is sparse.
claims.source_text: In patients with suspected GCA, glucocorticoids should be immediately initiated. The diagnostic work-up should not delay the initiation of treatment. For patients without visual manifestations we recommend a starting dose of 40 mg Prednisolone/day. In patients with visual involvement (visual loss, diplopia, amaurosis fugax, and blurred vision), we recommend starting with 60 mg Prednisolone/day. A single dose of 500 mg × 1 methylprednisolone iv followed by Prednisolone 60 mg/day may be individually considered, but the evidence is sparse
claims.locator: Norwegian Society of Rheumatology GCA working group (Haaversen et al.), Frontiers in Medicine, 'Norwegian society of rheumatology recommendations on diagnosis and treatment of patients with giant cell arteritis', published 6 January 2023 (volume 2022), https://europepmc.org/article/PMC/PMC9853546, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Taper:** by 5 mg every 2nd week to 20 mg/day, then 2.5 mg every 3rd week to 10 mg/day, then 1.25 mg every 3rd week to 5 mg/day. From 60 mg/day, first reduce by 10 mg every week to 40 mg/day.
claims.source_text: In patients with GCA, Prednisolone should be tapered by 5 mg every 2nd week till 20 mg/day, after that with 2.5 mg every 3rd week till 10 mg/day, and after that with 1.25 mg every 3rd week to 5 mg/day. … When starting with dose 60 mg/day, Prednisolone should be tapered by 10 mg every week till 40 mg/day, thereafter tapering as described above
claims.locator: Norwegian Society of Rheumatology GCA working group (Haaversen et al.), Frontiers in Medicine, 'Norwegian society of rheumatology recommendations on diagnosis and treatment of patients with giant cell arteritis', published 6 January 2023 (volume 2022), https://europepmc.org/article/PMC/PMC9853546, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Continue 5 mg/day for at least 1 year from the start;** taper further only individually, after at least 1 year in remission.
claims.source_text: We recommend continuing treatment with 5 mg/day at least for 1 year after initiation of Prednisolone. Further tapering can be considered on an individual basis if the patient has been in remission for at least 1 year.
claims.locator: Norwegian Society of Rheumatology GCA working group (Haaversen et al.), Frontiers in Medicine, 'Norwegian society of rheumatology recommendations on diagnosis and treatment of patients with giant cell arteritis', published 6 January 2023 (volume 2022), https://europepmc.org/article/PMC/PMC9853546, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **S2 (ACR): start high-dose oral steroids daily** (not on alternate days, and not a moderate dose unless steroid toxicity risk is high and the risk of visual loss is low). Without cranial ischaemia, oral beats IV pulses; **with threatened visual loss, use IV pulse steroids.**
claims.locator: American College of Rheumatology and Vasculitis Foundation (Maz M, Chung SA, Abril A, et al.), Arthritis & Rheumatology 73(8):1349-1365 (doi 10.1002/art.41774), NIH author manuscript NIHMS2099608, '2021 American College of Rheumatology/Vasculitis Foundation Guideline for the Management of Giant Cell Arteritis and Takayasu Arteritis', published online 8 July 2021, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12344528/, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: **S2: how long to continue steroids is not established;** it should follow the patient's values and preferences, the number of flares and steroid toxicity.
claims.locator: American College of Rheumatology and Vasculitis Foundation (Maz M, Chung SA, Abril A, et al.), Arthritis & Rheumatology 73(8):1349-1365 (doi 10.1002/art.41774), NIH author manuscript NIHMS2099608, '2021 American College of Rheumatology/Vasculitis Foundation Guideline for the Management of Giant Cell Arteritis and Takayasu Arteritis', published online 8 July 2021, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12344528/, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: **Relapse:** raise prednisolone to the last effective dose, or higher depending on severity. Confirm relapse by imaging (preferably ultrasound) and/or blood tests where possible.
claims.source_text: If the patients suffers a relapse, we recommend an increase in Prednisolone dose to the last effective dose, or a higher dose based on the severity of the relapse and an individual assessment. … In GCA patients who suffer a relapse, the relapse should, if possible, be confirmed by an imaging modality, preferably ultrasound, and/or laboratory tests
claims.locator: Norwegian Society of Rheumatology GCA working group (Haaversen et al.), Frontiers in Medicine, 'Norwegian society of rheumatology recommendations on diagnosis and treatment of patients with giant cell arteritis', published 6 January 2023 (volume 2022), https://europepmc.org/article/PMC/PMC9853546, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Refractory disease or major relapse: consider methotrexate 20 mg/week, preferably subcutaneous,** adjusted for age and kidney function.
claims.source_text: In patients with refractory disease or a major relapse (Table 7), initiation of Methotrexate (MTX), preferably subcutaneously, 20 mg/week, should be considered. The dose should be adjusted according to the patient's age and kidney function.
claims.locator: Norwegian Society of Rheumatology GCA working group (Haaversen et al.), Frontiers in Medicine, 'Norwegian society of rheumatology recommendations on diagnosis and treatment of patients with giant cell arteritis', published 6 January 2023 (volume 2022), https://europepmc.org/article/PMC/PMC9853546, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Tocilizumab 162 mg/week subcutaneously** if methotrexate is not tolerated or relapse occurs on it. Leflunomide or azathioprine have scarce evidence; there is no robust evidence for TNF inhibitors or other biologics.
claims.source_text: Tocilizumab (TCZ) 162 mg/week sc should be considered if the patient is not tolerating MTX or suffer a relapse while on MTX (according to the Norwegian Tender System). Leflunomide or Azathioprine may be considered, but evidence supporting their use is scarce. There is currently no robust evidence supporting the use of TNF-α inhibitors or other biologics than TCZ in patients with GCA.
claims.locator: Norwegian Society of Rheumatology GCA working group (Haaversen et al.), Frontiers in Medicine, 'Norwegian society of rheumatology recommendations on diagnosis and treatment of patients with giant cell arteritis', published 6 January 2023 (volume 2022), https://europepmc.org/article/PMC/PMC9853546, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Relapsing or refractory disease: reconsider the diagnosis** (for example malignancy or an autoinflammatory syndrome).
claims.source_text: In GCA patients with relapsing or refractory disease, alternative diagnoses should be considered (e.g., malignancy, autoinflammatory syndromes).
claims.locator: Norwegian Society of Rheumatology GCA working group (Haaversen et al.), Frontiers in Medicine, 'Norwegian society of rheumatology recommendations on diagnosis and treatment of patients with giant cell arteritis', published 6 January 2023 (volume 2022), https://europepmc.org/article/PMC/PMC9853546, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **S2 (ACR) differs from S1: it suggests tocilizumab with steroids from diagnosis** rather than steroids alone, for its steroid-sparing effect (GiACTA); methotrexate with steroids, or steroids alone, remain options, and abatacept if these fail. Cost and limited long-term data may restrict tocilizumab.
claims.locator: American College of Rheumatology and Vasculitis Foundation (Maz M, Chung SA, Abril A, et al.), Arthritis & Rheumatology 73(8):1349-1365 (doi 10.1002/art.41774), NIH author manuscript NIHMS2099608, '2021 American College of Rheumatology/Vasculitis Foundation Guideline for the Management of Giant Cell Arteritis and Takayasu Arteritis', published online 8 July 2021, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12344528/, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: **Active large-vessel (extracranial) disease: add a steroid-sparing drug,** preferably tocilizumab; methotrexate if tocilizumab is unsuitable (recurrent infections, past bowel perforation or diverticulitis, or cost).
claims.locator: American College of Rheumatology and Vasculitis Foundation (Maz M, Chung SA, Abril A, et al.), Arthritis & Rheumatology 73(8):1349-1365 (doi 10.1002/art.41774), NIH author manuscript NIHMS2099608, '2021 American College of Rheumatology/Vasculitis Foundation Guideline for the Management of Giant Cell Arteritis and Takayasu Arteritis', published online 8 July 2021, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12344528/, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: **S2 on relapse:** relapse on moderate or high-dose steroids → add a steroid-sparing drug; relapse with cranial ischaemia → raise steroids and add one; cranial relapse → prefer tocilizumab to methotrexate. Polymyalgia-type relapses may need only a higher steroid dose.
claims.locator: American College of Rheumatology and Vasculitis Foundation (Maz M, Chung SA, Abril A, et al.), Arthritis & Rheumatology 73(8):1349-1365 (doi 10.1002/art.41774), NIH author manuscript NIHMS2099608, '2021 American College of Rheumatology/Vasculitis Foundation Guideline for the Management of Giant Cell Arteritis and Takayasu Arteritis', published online 8 July 2021, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12344528/, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: **Worsening limb or organ ischaemia: escalate immunosuppression before surgery,** unless an aortic aneurysm is at high risk of rupture or tissue infarction is imminent. Plan vascular procedures jointly with the vascular surgeon, and cover them with high-dose steroids if the disease is active.
claims.locator: American College of Rheumatology and Vasculitis Foundation (Maz M, Chung SA, Abril A, et al.), Arthritis & Rheumatology 73(8):1349-1365 (doi 10.1002/art.41774), NIH author manuscript NIHMS2099608, '2021 American College of Rheumatology/Vasculitis Foundation Guideline for the Management of Giant Cell Arteritis and Takayasu Arteritis', published online 8 July 2021, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12344528/, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: **Check bone density in new-onset GCA** and treat osteoporosis risk. **Aspirin is not routine** unless there is a cardiovascular reason.
claims.source_text: Giant cell arteritis patients with new-onset disease should be referred to a measurement of bone mass density. … In patients with GCA, we do not routinely recommend using Acetylsalicylic acid unless cardiovascular reasons support its use
claims.locator: Norwegian Society of Rheumatology GCA working group (Haaversen et al.), Frontiers in Medicine, 'Norwegian society of rheumatology recommendations on diagnosis and treatment of patients with giant cell arteritis', published 6 January 2023 (volume 2022), https://europepmc.org/article/PMC/PMC9853546, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Review monthly until remission, then at 3 months, 6 months, and yearly.**
claims.source_text: In GCA patients, follow-up should be continued every month until remission is achieved. Thereafter follow-up at 3 months, 6 months, and thereafter yearly.
claims.locator: Norwegian Society of Rheumatology GCA working group (Haaversen et al.), Frontiers in Medicine, 'Norwegian society of rheumatology recommendations on diagnosis and treatment of patients with giant cell arteritis', published 6 January 2023 (volume 2022), https://europepmc.org/article/PMC/PMC9853546, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **S2: no statin to treat GCA itself; add aspirin only for critical or flow-limiting vertebral or carotid disease.** Statins for cardiovascular risk are a separate decision.
claims.locator: American College of Rheumatology and Vasculitis Foundation (Maz M, Chung SA, Abril A, et al.), Arthritis & Rheumatology 73(8):1349-1365 (doi 10.1002/art.41774), NIH author manuscript NIHMS2099608, '2021 American College of Rheumatology/Vasculitis Foundation Guideline for the Management of Giant Cell Arteritis and Takayasu Arteritis', published online 8 July 2021, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12344528/, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: ⚠️ **S2: keep monitoring long term in remission** (strong recommendation, because missed disease can be catastrophic). **A rise in ESR or CRP alone is not a reason to escalate;** watch more closely instead.
claims.locator: American College of Rheumatology and Vasculitis Foundation (Maz M, Chung SA, Abril A, et al.), Arthritis & Rheumatology 73(8):1349-1365 (doi 10.1002/art.41774), NIH author manuscript NIHMS2099608, '2021 American College of Rheumatology/Vasculitis Foundation Guideline for the Management of Giant Cell Arteritis and Takayasu Arteritis', published online 8 July 2021, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12344528/, retrieved 2026-09-24
